title: Backtracking: Combination Sum
oneLiner: All combinations of candidates that add up to a target, each candidate reusable. Backtrack with a start index so every combination is built in one order only.
keyTakeaway: Choose, recurse, un-choose, with two twists. Recursing with the same index i (not i + 1) lets a number be reused. Never going back to an earlier index means [2, 2, 3] is built once instead of as every permutation. Sorting the candidates lets you stop the loop as soon as a candidate is larger than what remains.
explanation:
candidates are distinct positive integers. Return every combination of them that sums to target, where each candidate may be used any number of times. Order within a combination doesn't matter and each combination appears once. For [2, 3, 6, 7] and target 7 the answer is [[2, 2, 3], [7]]. The grader sorts your combinations before comparing, so any order of output is fine.

This is the Subsets backtracking shape with a running remainder. backtrack(start, remaining): if remaining is 0, record a copy of the current path. Otherwise for each index i from start onwards: put candidates[i] on the path, recurse with backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i]), then take it off again.

Two details carry the whole problem. Recursing with i rather than i + 1 is what allows reuse: after picking 2 you may pick 2 again. Starting the loop at start rather than 0 is what prevents duplicates: once you have moved past 2 to 3, you never come back to 2, so [3, 2, 2] can't be built after [2, 2, 3]. Each combination is generated in exactly one order, non-decreasing by index.

Pruning: sort the candidates first. Then when candidates[i] > remaining, every later candidate is too big as well, so break out of the loop instead of recursing into dead ends.

The output can be exponential in size, so the running time is too. A rough bound is O(n^(T/m)), for target T and smallest candidate m, which is the depth of the deepest path. The recursion stack and the current path hold at most T/m values.

The visualization runs [2, 3, 6, 7] with target 7, showing the call stack as (path, remaining).

recognitionSignals: "Find all combinations" that reach a target sum, with unlimited reuse.
Output is a list of lists and its size can be exponential: backtracking.
gotchas: Recursing with i + 1 forbids reuse (that is Combination Sum II); recursing from 0 creates permutations of the same combination.
Recording current instead of a copy: every recorded list ends up empty after backtracking.
Without sorting, break is wrong (a later, smaller candidate might still fit); use continue, or sort first.
confusableWith: Subsets records every path; this records only paths whose sum hits the target, and lets values repeat.
Coin Change Ways counts the same combinations with DP instead of listing them, which is far cheaper when you only need the number.

complexity.note: Exponential: the search tree branches up to n ways at each level and is as deep as target / smallest candidate, so a common bound is O(n^(T/m)). The stack and the current path hold at most T/m values, which is at most T.

referenceSolutions.python:
def combination_sum(candidates, target):
    candidates = sorted(candidates)  # sorted, so a too-big candidate ends the loop
    result = []
    path = []

    def backtrack(start, remaining):
        if remaining == 0:
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):  # never an earlier index: no duplicate orders
            if candidates[i] > remaining:
                break
            path.append(candidates[i])
            backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i])  # i, not i + 1: reuse allowed
            path.pop()

    backtrack(0, target)
    return result
